messages.body_plain:
If you're wanting to predict abundance (as opposed to understand the underlying mechanisms of abundance, i.e., "interpreting coefficients"), then using principal components is fine as long as the prediction intervals meet your desired levels of precision.

If "explaining" predictions is the objective, then using principal components or throwing out highly correlated predictors just hides the multicollinearity issue.  "Explaining" needs lots of thinking and subject matter knowledge and automatic processes such as principal components tends to bypass the thinking and subject matter knowledge components.  (If all it took was a numeric procedure, why would we statisticians need you guys?)

Things are not certainly as black-and-white as maybe I've implied above, but if prediction is the objective, then you're not as restricted to what you can do and in the end, good enough predictions are what counts.  (Assuming one knows what "good enough" is.)

Jim

I used a PCA to determine which wetland classifications explained the most variation. The first 3 PCs correspond to 4 common and biologically important wetland classifications and explained close to 80% of the variation in my data. I am attempting to predict based on the proportion of each PC within each surveyed site. I used a PCA because my model originally wouldn't run with so many abundance covariates and I needed a repeatable way to reduce landcover classifications. > > If you are interested in predicting abundance, then you want those predictions based only on the abundance predictors.  pcount (and other routines in unmarked) allow one to get estimates "free and clear" of the nuisance caused by less-than-perfect detection.  While the detection parameters certainly influence the observed counts, the predictions are about what one would observe if detection was perfect.  Now if the detection probabilities are low that that will generally increase the standard errors for the estimates of abundance and the associated parameters.  So there is an influence in that respect.
> >

> >

Performing manipulations on a large set of variables in complete isolation of what one wants to predict makes little sense to me. messages.body_plain:
Hi unmarked google group!

I have a question regarding data sets in which multiple observation types are used. However, I'm not entirely certain if a multi-method model is the most appropriate model for me. I have searched this group and the UNMARKED documentation, but could not find an answer to this question. If you're willing, I've detailed the nature of my study and data below.

The data are counts of reptiles and amphibians from cover board surveys. During these surveys, three types of cover boards were checked: wood, aluminum, and mesh. The goal of the study is to determine if the third type, mesh, confers different detection probabilities of reptiles and amphibians than the standard cover types, wood and aluminum. We do not wish to quantify any state processes, but rather simply model detection. Explanation: this mesh cover type is a prototype developed by my colleagues and I, and we hypothesize that it will yield greater probability of certain species than other methods.

This study took place at three independent sites (at least 60 miles apart). At each site there are 20 replicates of each cover type, yielding a total of 180 cover boards over all. Cover boards were sampled 6 times within a single season, however due to logistical restraints some cover arrays were not sampled. We also collected several covariates at the cover board (observation) level (e.g. soil moisture, surface temp, presence of ants/mammals/burrows). Therefore, we have covariates for each cover board, across types, sites, and sample events. Although, due to aforementioned logistical constraints, some covariate data are missing (especially in the instances where observations were not made).

Question 1: Because we are only interested in modeling detection, is it appropriate to treat individual cover boards or replicates as "sites"? We believe the likelihood of detection at any single cover board is independent of other cover boards.
Question 2: Should I implement a multi-method model to model detection probabilities for each cover type, or instead use cover board type as a covariate for detection? If a multi-method is more appropriate, does UNMARKED provide such a model?
Question 3 (or 2a): Because the data are counts rather than presence/absence, would a N-mixture model the appropriate type? If so, I'm not aware of a N-mixture model incorporating multiple methods. Does such a model exist?

Thank you in advance for you time and patience!!

-Alex

Setting the argument 'type' to either the state (= occupancy or abundance) or detection and providing a data set with the values of the covariates at which you want to predict will provide you with what you want.

This is actually shown in the unmarked overview vignette, here:  https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/unmarked/vignettes/unmarked.pdf

messages.subject_clean: Time-of-detection method using multinomPois function
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

>
> 1. Is the correct data format structure: tabulated capture histories for each point count site such that I have a matrix of 479 rows by 30 columns (i.e. number of observable encounter histories from 5 time intervals)?

30 columns seems correct for a single-closed period. Because you have repeated visits and time-of-detection, you might choose to fit a generalized multinomial mixture (with parameters for availability and detection given availability), in which case you might want 479*2 years rows and 30*3 visits columns. If you fit a strictly closed model (say, with a call to multinomPois), I think you'd have to format this as 30 columns with 479*2*3 rows. If you want to fit a model with explicit dynamics (i.e., parameters corresponding to changes in abundance between years, or between surveys and years), you'll have to code something up. Any of these approaches might be okay, depending upon your specific objectives/foci/etc.

> 2. Will I need to define the piFun for the time-of-detection method? Would it look like this below?
>

That pi function looks correct for a constant (M0) detection model, without looking closely to see if there are typos or missing encounter history types or anything.

> 3. Would the obsToY argument in the multinomPois function be: o2y <- matrix(1, 5, 30)?

Depends upon how you construct the unmarked frame. The number of rows here corresponds to the number of columns in some observation covariate: for the pi function above, this argument might work if any covariate you wanted to work with relates to time interval 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. If you don't have any observation covariates, then I guess 1 row would be fine. If you stack the data and treat each site*year*visit as a separate row in the observation matrix, date and time are actually functioning as site covariates. If you have 2*497 rows and 3*30 columns in y, then I *think* (for time and date, at least) that o2y <- matrix(1, 6, 30) will work.

>
> 4. In the cap-recap vignette, the time (time.1) and date (date.1) of only the first surveys of the the year were included in the siteCovs argument. However, my data consist of 3 surveys a year - how would I include time (i.e. time.1, time.2, time.3) and date (date.1, date.2, date.3) as obsCovs?

You can do this in a gmultimix unmarked frame easily. Not in a stacked unmarked frame used to fit a strictly closed model--these, again, would be siteCovs.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Alex,

>
> Question 1: Because we are only interested in modeling detection, is it appropriate to treat individual cover boards or replicates as "sites"? We believe the likelihood of detection at any single cover board is independent of other cover boards.
>
> Question 2: Should I implement a multi-method model to model detection probabilities for each cover type, or instead use cover board type as a covariate for detection? If a multi-method is more appropriate, does UNMARKED provide such a model?

I don't quite follow the study design, but maybe this helps. Typically, "site" delineates areas/sampling locations within which the value of the state parameter is distinct. A multi-method model (at least, the specific variants related to Nichols et al. 2008) typically assumes that multiple detectors (same type, different type, whatever) are nested within sites. If each cover board is truly distinct/independent, than it may make more sense to deal with this using a site level covariate. Alternatively, if different detectors operate at the same place but at distinct times, than it probably makes more sense to compare types using observation-level covariates.

> Question 3 (or 2a): Because the data are counts rather than presence/absence, would a N-mixture model the appropriate type? If so, I'm not aware of a N-mixture model incorporating multiple methods. Does such a model exist?

Using counts rather than splitting this into detection vs. not would be a more efficient use of the data (with caveats pertaining to identifiability in certain circumstances). I know people have worked out multi-detector N-mixtures, but nothing's published (as far as I know).

Hi all,

I am using two-pass visual surveys to estimate fish abundance using N-mixture models. I have 79 sites that were surveyed twice, and among-site counts range from 0 to 400 or so.

We have a high correlation of counts between passes at a given site (r2 = 0.97), and relatively little variation in our between-survey detection covariates. If I am following the AHM book (p. 224), am I correct in interpreting that the model has to (whether right or wrong) predict high detection under these conditions?

Estimated detection was high when using ZIP and Poisson distributions, but data were still overdispersed. Only the NB distribution lowers c-hat to < 4. However, we run into issues when using NB (the model is non-identifiable) that have been outlined elsewhere.

Thanks,
Andy

hi Andy,
 It should not necessarily predict high detection under these conditions.  One would expect it to produce unbiased estimates of detection if the model is properly specified. I don't have any specific recommendations to dealing with that problem other than mark a subset of fish.

andy

Researcher - Bioinformatics (with relation to Genetics, Ecology and Wildlife Conservation)

University of Ljubljana, Biotechnical Faculty, Dpt. of Biology, Animal Ecology Research Group

Application Deadline: 7 May 2018, or until the position is filled

A full time post-doc or doctorate researcher position is available at Dpt. for Biology, Animal Ecology Research Group. We encourage applications from highly-motivated post docs or researchers with good programming skills. We will also consider candidates with the required skill set but without a finished PhD, with a possibility to enroll in graduate studies at our institution.

Starting date: as soon as possible, but no later than June 2018.

Duration: 1 year, with possibility of extension.

Location: Ljubljana, Slovenia.

Keywords: Bioinformatics, Genetics, Wildlife Conservation, Ecology, Brown bear, Ursus arctos, Eurasian lynx, Lynx lynx.

JOB DESCRIPTION

We invite applications from highly motivated candidates with advanced computer programming / informatics background and passion for wildlife ecology and conservation. The work will be related to two international Life projects, LIFE DINALP BEAR and LIFE LYNX, with strong emphasis on conservation genetics of brown bear (Ursus arctos) and Eurasian lynx (Lynx lynx).

Specifically, the candidate will work on programming a stochastic simulation system for brown bear population dynamics in Northern Dinaric Mountains and stochastic genetics / population dynamics simulations of lynx population augmentation. Some programming work will also be required in optimization/programming of bioinformatics pipelines for analysis of next-generation sequencing data.

Since we're a multidisciplinary and dynamic group, the candidate will also have a possibility to engage in other activities of the group (e.g. fieldwork, other research) when the main obligations will permit. The candidate will also have the opportunity (but not obligation) to develop hers/his own personal research interests within the scope of the work we do. We are looking for candidates that are able to work independently on specific tasks but still function as a part of the team. The working language is English, everyone in the research group speaks it and we have other foreigners working with us.

RESEARCH GROUP DESCRIPTION

We’re a dynamic, multidisciplinary group that combines “classic” approaches in animal ecology and conservation with molecular genetics and social sciences. While some of our projects are oriented in basic ecology, much of our work is conservation oriented, mainly in conservation of European large carnivores: the wolf, the bear and the lynx. We have considerable laboratory, computing and field resources, and engage in a variety of research projects.

Some of our past/current projects (the ones that have nice webpages J):

http://fp7hunt.net/

http://www.volkovi.si

http://dinalpbear.eu

https://www.lifelynx.eu/

EXPECTED SALARY, LIVING

The total net salary would be between 1100€ – 1500€, depending on the academic title (different for BSc, MSc or PhD).

The salary is not great compared to western European countries, but enough for a decent living in Slovenia. Living costs in Slovenia are not that high, and Ljubljana is a nice place to live – there are both mountains and the Adriatic Sea close by. A one to two hour drive can take you sailing / swimming / diving / windsurfing / fishing in summer, and a 1/2 hour drive skiing in winter, or hiking / rock climbing in summer. The city is very green, and wildlife areas start right at the outskirts (we've had bears enter city proper). It's a small city which makes it easy to move around, it's relatively bike-friendly, but being a capital we get much more culture (concerts, events, festivals...) than most other cities of this size. It's also clean and safe.

https://www.visitljubljana.com

REQUIRED SKILLS AND LEVEL

The skills listed below are a must to apply to this position. Please list references or some verifiable information, or explain how we can confirm your proficiency.

Biology / Life Sciences or Mathematics / Statistics / Computer sciences background, with appropriate achieved degree (typically a PhD, but MSc and BSc candidates will be considered).

Computer programming, advanced level. Our preferred programming languages are R, Python and C/C++. Since we do a lot of our simulation programming and analysis in R, any candidate should be either already an advanced R user or demonstrably (e.g. through showing proficiency in another programming language) willing/able to learn R to an advanced level through self-study in a very short time.

Linux use and administration, intermediate/advanced – we have a small HPC running CentOS Linux as our primary number cruncher which we administer ourselves, and the candidate should be able to do intermediate maintenance tasks to keep it running. He or she should also be able to use bioinformatics tools in Linux, so an understanding of this OS is a must.

DESIRED SKILLS

Any of these skills would help you in getting the job:

Manipulation and analysis of next-generation sequencing data.

Experience in molecular genetics and analysis of genetic data.

Experience in genomics and analysis of genomic data.

Advanced statistical modelling.

Modelling of population dynamics.

GIS

APPLICATION PROCEDURE

An interested candidate should send his/her C.V. and a cover letter explaining why he or she would like this job to tomaz.s...@gmail.com. Selected candidates will be invited for an interview, in person if feasible or via Skype.
